articles.title: Proxies or a scraping API? How to choose for public web data
articles.excerpt: If you collect public web data, you will hit the same question sooner or later: do you route your own requests through proxies, or hand the whole job to a scraping API? Both work. They solve different…
articles.body: If you collect public web data, you will hit the same question sooner or later: do you route your own requests through proxies, or hand the whole job to a scraping API? Both work. They solve different problems. What proxies give you A proxy sends your request from a different IP address. You keep full control: your own code, your own parsing, your own retry rules. The common types differ in where the IP comes from: Residential proxies use IPs assigned to home internet connections. They look like ordinary visitors, so they suit sites that treat datacenter traffic with suspicion. ISP proxies sit between the two: hosted in a datacenter but registered under an internet provider. Datacenter proxies come from server infrastructure.

articles.title: Your Excel/VBA tool outgrew Excel: 6 signs to rebuild it as a desktop or web app (and what to keep)
articles.excerpt: Your Excel macro runs the factory. Then the one person who understands it goes on holiday. Most small firms have a workbook like this. It started as a sheet to track orders, stock or shifts. Then it g…
articles.body: Your Excel macro runs the factory. Then the one person who understands it goes on holiday. Most small firms have a workbook like this. It started as a sheet to track orders, stock or shifts. Then it got macros, then forms, then a button that emails the weekly report. Now the business runs on it, and nobody wants to touch it. Excel is a good tool. Many workbooks should stay workbooks. But some reach a point where every week you keep them in Excel costs more than a rebuild. Here are six signs, and what to keep when you rebuild. 1. Two people need it at the same time "Can you close the file? I need to save." If people take turns, or keep their own copies and merge them on Friday, the workbook is acting as a database. It is not one.

articles.title: Your Product Manager Celebrates the NPS Going Up and You Do Not Know What It Tells You
articles.excerpt: The quarterly review opens with a slide. Net Promoter Score up from twenty four to thirty one. People clap. You built half of the features released that quarter, and you have no idea whether the users…
articles.body: The quarterly review opens with a slide. Net Promoter Score up from twenty four to thirty one. People clap. You built half of the features released that quarter, and you have no idea whether the users liked them, or what the number actually measures. It is worth understanding, because it is one of the most common pieces of customer feedback a company collects. The idea comes from Fred Reichheld, who described it in a 2003 Harvard Business Review article called The One Number You Need to Grow. Customers are asked one question. How likely is it that you would recommend us to a friend or colleague, on a scale from nought to ten. People who answer nine or ten are promoters. Seven or eight are passives. Nought to six are detractors.

articles.title: We minified our despatch email template and the mail relay started putting spaces in the middle of tracking links
articles.excerpt: When a parcel leaves one of our depots, our notification service emails the customer a despatch confirmation with the carrier's tracking link. The service is old. It builds the raw message from a temp…
articles.body: When a parcel leaves one of our depots, our notification service emails the customer a despatch confirmation with the carrier's tracking link. The service is old. It builds the raw message from a template file that holds the headers and an HTML body, and one of those headers, written in 2016, says Content-Transfer-Encoding: 8bit. The messages go out through the Postfix 3.7 relay that Debian 12 ships, on one of our servers. In October a front end colleague tidied our email templates and added a build step that minified the HTML, to make the messages smaller. The despatch email's body became one line of about eleven thousand characters. Within a week customer service had a pattern. Some customers clicked the tracking link and got the carrier's page saying the parcel did not exist.

articles.title: I asked AI for Christmas snow. It looked fake, so I dug up my college math
articles.excerpt: Short on time? Jump to the examples and the skill file at the end. So, winter's coming, and I got asked to make it snow on the world map in our mobile app. Cute little feature. I figured I'd ask my AI…
articles.body: Short on time? Jump to the examples and the skill file at the end. So, winter's coming, and I got asked to make it snow on the world map in our mobile app. Cute little feature. I figured I'd ask my AI agent, tweak a couple of numbers and move on. The snow showed up in about a minute. And it looked... wrong. Flakes bunched up in little clumps, the whole sky swayed left and right like one big curtain, and flakes faded out and popped right back in on the same spot. It took me a while to put my finger on why it bugged me so much. Then it clicked. This is the snow on basically every website: random x, random y, fall, jump back to the top. Everyone writes it that way, so of course the AI does too.

articles.title: ChatGPT and Codex will share usage limits for paid users starting in December
articles.excerpt: Using one AI tool could limit how much you can use another.
articles.body: TL;DR Starting in December, ChatGPT, Work, and Codex will share a single usage allowance across Plus, Pro, and Business plans. Usage will be measured in tokens rather than messages, with more advanced models and complex tasks consuming more of your allowance. Instant chat will be exempt from the shared allowance, but OpenAI hasn’t disclosed how large the new limits will be. ChatGPT has grown into much more than a chatbot , with OpenAI introducing tools like Work and Codex to help users tackle everything from building presentations to developing apps. Until now, you could use these tools without worrying about how they would affect your regular ChatGPT allowance. But as OpenAI brings Chat and Work together, it’s also changing how much you can do with your paid subscription.

articles.body: SpaceX launched another classified mission for the U.S. Space Force (USSF) today (Nov. 24), sending an unknown payload toward orbit from California. A Falcon 9 rocket lifted off from Vandenberg Space Force Base's Space Launch Complex-4E at TK11:08 a.m. ET (1508 GMT) , carrying the U.S. Space Force's USSF-266 mission. It was the fourth mission SpaceX has launched for the military branch this month. While details about the mission's payload weren't disclosed, it's the fifth space launch in support of U.S. national security in the last two weeks, and comes amid efforts by the Space Force to expand its communications and tracking capabilities.

articles.title: On this day in space! Nov. 24, 1947: The US Navy launches the 1st Aerobee sounding rocket, but it didn't reach space
articles.excerpt: On Nov. 24, 1947, the U.S. Navy launched the first Aerobee rocket into the sky, but it never reached space. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Nov. 24, 1947, the U.S. Navy launched the first Aerobee rocket into the sky, but it never reached space. Aerobee was a suborbital sounding rocket designed to study Earth's atmosphere . After World War 2, the United States started reusing erman V-2 rockets for this kind of research. When they started running out of V-2 rockets , the United States constructed its own rockets that were similar but cheaper to build and to launch. In the weeks leading up to the first Aerobee mission, three test flights were launched. Those tests used a dummy version of Aerobee with a live booster to see if the two stages would separate properly. On Aerobee's first real flight, the rocket flew about 35 miles high. That's below the 62-mile (100 kilometers) upper limit for the boundary of space .
